WS8 · Editorial operations and QA leadership

Running a Curriculum Release

How I would run quality assurance for a team of contract editors shipping one curriculum unit in print and digital. The scenario, people, dates and numbers are invented to show the method.

Simulated scenario. The publisher, the editors and every number on this page are fictional. This sample shows how I would set up and run a QA process. It is not a record of a team I have led.
Role in scenario
Editorial QA lead
Scope
Grade 4 ELA unit: 10 lessons, assessment, student book pages, digital slides
Team
4 contract editors, 1 proofreader, typesetting vendor
Timeline
3 weeks to print-ready files
Label
Simulated scenario
Look at this first: the reviewer calibration guide. Inconsistent severity ratings across contractors are the most common reason QA data cannot be trusted, and this is how I would prevent it.

1. Editorial brief

DeliverableGrade 4 Unit 3, "Nature's Engineers": teacher guide (10 lessons), 24 student book pages, end-of-unit assessment, 10 slide decks
Quality barZero critical and zero major issues at print release; minor issues under 1 per page; all standards quoted verbatim; all facts sourced
StyleHouse style guide v4 plus the unit glossary; Chicago for anything the guide does not cover
AccessibilityDigital: WCAG 2.2 AA as the reference checklist; alt text for every image; no meaning carried by color alone. Print: minimum 12 pt body text in student pages
Out of scopeChanging the scope and sequence; new texts (any request goes through change control)
DatesWeek 1 content review · Week 2 revisions and first proofs · Week 3 second proofs and print release

2. QA workflow and checkpoints

StageOwnerEntry criteriaChecksExit criteria
0. Kickoff and calibrationQA leadBrief signed offCalibration exercise; agreement on severityReviewers within one severity level on 9 of 10 samples
1. Content reviewEditors A–D, one lesson set eachManuscript lockedAccuracy and sources; alignment; pedagogy; biasEvery issue logged with category and severity
2. Cross-checkEditors swap 20% of each other's lessonsStage 1 logs completeSecond-reader sample for missed issuesMiss rate recorded; recalibrate if over 15%
3. Author revisionsWriters, with queries from QA leadConsolidated query listEach query answered or escalatedAll critical and major issues closed
4. First proofsProofreader + editor of recordTypeset pages receivedText matches manuscript; layout; art and captions; page referencesCorrections marked; vendor query sent
5. Second proofsProofreaderCorrections returnedEvery correction verified; no new errors introducedZero critical or major; signed print release
6. Digital checkEditor CSlides exportedAccessibility checklist; links; slide numberingChecklist complete

4. Reviewer calibration guide

Before reviewing, every editor rates the same ten sample issues alone, then we compare. Where ratings differ by more than one level, we discuss until we agree on the rule, and the rule goes into this guide.

SeverityRuleExample
CriticalA student or teacher would learn something false, an assessment would score wrongly, or content could cause harm or legal exposure.Wrong answer key; a factual error in a passage; an image used without permission.
MajorWeakens learning or assessment, or would confuse most users, but does not teach an error.A question refers to a heading that does not exist; practice that does not match the objective; a standard misquoted.
MinorShould be fixed for quality and consistency; does not change what students learn.Style inconsistency; a missing item in a materials list; slide number off by one.

Calibration exercise results (simulated)

Sample issueABCDAgreedRule added
Passage says hail falls "when the air is very cold"MajCritCritMinCriticalAny fact students would learn wrongly is critical, even if it is one clause.
Footer text contrast 4.27:1 on a slideMinMinMajMinMajor (digital)Fails a WCAG AA check on student-facing material: major in digital, minor in teacher-only notes.
Vocabulary item tests a word taught in the lessonMinMajMajMajMajorAn item that measures recall of a lesson instead of the skill is a validity issue: major.
"L.4.4.a" instead of house style "L.4.4a"MinMinMinMinMinor—

The sample issues are real issues from WS7 and WS10. The editors' ratings are simulated.

5. Vendor and author query templates

Author query

Query ID: AQ-U3-L5-02
Location: Lesson 5, step 3, paragraph 2
Issue: The text says the story "never states" what the white cloud is; the teacher note on page 47 states it directly. Students reading the teacher-facing slide would see the answer.
Question: Can we move the note to the speaker notes only?
Needed by: Wed 12:00 · Severity: Major

Typesetter query

Query ID: TQ-U3-SB-14
Pages: Student book 12–13
Issue: Paragraph numbers 4–6 are missing on page 13, but Questions 3 and 4 refer to them.
Requested fix: Restore paragraph numbers in the left margin, same style as page 12.
Return by: Thu proofs · Severity: Major

Permissions and art query

Query ID: PQ-U3-07
Item: Beaver dam photo, Lesson 1
Issue: Credit line missing; source and license not recorded in the rights log.
Request: Confirm source and license or replace with a public-domain image; send the credit line.
Severity: Critical until resolved

Escalation

Any query not answered by its deadline goes to the managing editor in the daily status note with the impact on the release date. Two missed deadlines from one vendor trigger a call, not another email.

6. Change request

RequestCR-03: Replace Text 5 ("When Engineers Cause Trouble") with a shorter text for Grade 4.
Requested byPilot teacher feedback via product team
ImpactAffects Lesson 6, assessment items 17 and 18, the synthesis chart in Lesson 7. New text needs fact check and rights clearance. Estimated 3 editor days; pushes print release by 4 days.
Alternatives(a) Keep the text; add a chunked reading guide (1 day, no date change). (b) Replace after this print run, in the digital version first.
RecommendationOption (a) now, (b) for the next revision. The text is a deliberate stretch text and the unit's knowledge progression depends on it.
DecisionApproved: option (a). Logged as D-05.

8. Status updates

Subject: Unit 3 QA status, end of week 1: on track, one risk

Summary: Content review is complete for all lessons and the assessment. We logged 142 issues: 2 critical, 19 major, 121 minor. Print release date holds.

Risk: Lessons 4–6 have two unanswered author queries due Wednesday. If they slip past Thursday, first proofs for those lessons move a day. I'll confirm Thursday morning.

Decision needed: none this week.

Pattern worth knowing: 11 of the 19 major issues are practice tasks that don't match the lesson objective. I've added a check for this to the writer checklist for Unit 4.

Subject: Unit 3 QA status, mid-week 2: assessment blocked, date at risk by 1 day

Summary: Lessons and student pages are on track for Friday proofs. The assessment is blocked: item 14's answer key marks the wrong evidence sentence. Editor D has the fix; I need the item writer to confirm by noon tomorrow.

Decision needed by Thursday: if the item writer can't confirm, do we (a) ship with item 14 removed and rescore out of 29, or (b) hold the assessment one day? I recommend (b).

9. Quality scorecard (simulated data)

MeasureDefinitionTargetResult
Issues found before proofsShare of all issues caught at Stages 1–385% or more88% (142 of 161)
Escape rateCritical or major issues found after print release, per 100 pages00 (tracked for 60 days)
Reviewer miss rateIssues found by the second reader in the cross-check sampleUnder 15%12% overall; 22% for Lessons 4–6 before D-04
First-pass yieldComponents that passed second proofs with no new errors90%83% (5 of 6)
Query turnaroundMedian time for author and vendor queriesUnder 24 hours19 hours
On-time releasePrint files delivered by the agreed dateYesOne day late (D-03)

Retrospective, three actions: add "practice matches objective" and "assessed words not pre-taught" to the writer checklist; keep the 30% cross-check for any lesson set with a miss rate over 15%; move the assessment key check to Stage 1 so it can't block proofs.

10. Print proofing checklist

  • Text on the page matches the approved manuscript, word for word, in a side-by-side check.
  • Paragraph numbers, page references and question references all match.
  • No widows or orphans in student passages; no passage split mid-sentence across a spread.
  • Every image has a credit line matching the rights log; captions are correct.
  • Running heads, folios and lesson numbers are correct and in sequence.
  • Answer keys match the items as typeset, including option order.
  • Every correction from first proofs is made, and nothing else changed.

11. How I would lead the team

My leadership experience is as an academic leader: I have run curriculum and academic audit processes across campuses as a chief academic officer and dean, and I have managed teachers and staff. I have not managed a team of contract editors. This simulation shows how I would apply the same habits to one: agree on the rules before the work starts, make every issue visible in one place, give each contractor clear deadlines and fast answers, review a sample of everyone's work, and report risks early with a recommendation rather than a surprise.
